title: CI/CD for Machine Learning Systems
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# CI/CD for Machine Learning Systems

##### The Friday deploy that cost ₹22 lakh

A recommendation team in Bengaluru pushed a new ranking model on a Friday evening. Offline NDCG@10 was up 4.2% — a solid win. They deployed it to 100% of traffic and went home.

The model was better at ranking. It was also 180 ms slower at p99, because a new feature required a synchronous call to a service that had not been load-tested. Under weekend traffic, the recommendation carousel began timing out and rendering empty. Conversion dropped 31% for 38 hours before anyone connected the two events.

Estimated revenue impact: ₹22 lakh.

Every part of this was preventable, and none of it required better modelling. A canary at 5% would have surfaced the latency regression in twelve minutes. An automated rollback on error rate would have reverted it before anyone woke up. That is what CI/CD for ML buys: not faster deploys, but *safer* ones.

##### Three pipelines, not one

Traditional software has one artifact: code. ML has three, and they change independently.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph CI["CI — triggered by code push"]
        A[Lint, type-check] --> B[Unit tests]
        B --> C[Data contract tests]
        C --> D[Smoke train on sample]
        D --> E[Build + scan image]
    end
    subgraph CT["CT — triggered by schedule/drift/data"]
        F[Validate data] --> G[Train]
        G --> H[Evaluate vs retrained baseline]
        H --> I{Gates pass?}
        I -->|Yes| J[Register candidate]
    end
    subgraph CD["CD — triggered by approval"]
        K[Shadow] --> L[Canary 5%]
        L --> M[Progressive 25/50/100]
        M --> N[Promote alias]
        L -->|SLO breach| O[Auto rollback]
    end
    E --> CT
    J --> K
```

**CI** validates code. **CT** (continuous training) produces model candidates. **CD** deploys them safely. Conflating them — the classic "retrain and push to prod on a cron" — is how corrupt data becomes a production model with nobody in the loop.

##### CI for ML

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on: [pull_request, push]

jobs:
  quality:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
      - run: uv sync --frozen            # fails if the lockfile is stale
      - run: uv run ruff check src/ tests/
      - run: uv run mypy src/
      - run: uv run pytest tests/unit -q --cov=src --cov-fail-under=80

  data-contracts:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: uv run pytest tests/data -q      # pandera schemas on fixture data
      - run: uv run python -m scripts.check_feature_parity   # train vs serve

  smoke-train:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: uv run python -m src.train --config conf/ci.yaml --sample-rate 0.01
      - run: uv run pytest tests/behavioural -q    # directional + slice tests
      - uses: iterative/setup-cml@v2
      - run: |
          echo "## Smoke train metrics" > report.md
          uv run python -m scripts.metrics_table >> report.md
          cml comment create report.md          # posts results on the PR

  image:
    needs: [quality, data-contracts, smoke-train]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with: {push: true, tags: "${{ env.REG }}/trainer:${{ github.sha }}"}
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with: {image-ref: "${{ env.REG }}/trainer:${{ github.sha }}", exit-code: "1",
               severity: "CRITICAL,HIGH"}
```

The ML-specific pieces are `data-contracts`, `smoke-train` and the CML comment. The **feature parity check** is worth building explicitly: it computes a sample of features through both the training path and the serving path and asserts they match within tolerance. That one test prevents the most expensive class of ML bug.

The smoke train on 1% of data in under fifteen minutes catches wiring errors, missing dependencies and broken artifact passing — which is where most pipeline failures actually live. It is not testing model quality; it is testing that the pipeline runs.

Posting metrics as a PR comment via CML changes team behaviour: model changes become reviewable, with numbers, in the same place code is reviewed.

##### Model validation gates

```python
GATES = {
    "min_pr_auc": 0.38,
    "max_regression_vs_baseline": 0.005,
    "min_slice_pr_auc": 0.25,
    "max_fairness_gap": 0.05,
    "max_p99_latency_ms": 45,
    "max_model_mb": 400,
    "required_artifacts": ["model_card.yaml", "provenance.json"],
}

def validate_candidate(candidate, baseline) -> tuple[bool, list[str]]:
    f = []
    if candidate.pr_auc < GATES["min_pr_auc"]:
        f.append(f"pr_auc {candidate.pr_auc:.4f} below floor")
    if candidate.pr_auc < baseline.pr_auc - GATES["max_regression_vs_baseline"]:
        f.append(f"regression vs baseline {baseline.pr_auc:.4f}")
    if min(candidate.slices.values()) < GATES["min_slice_pr_auc"]:
        worst = min(candidate.slices, key=candidate.slices.get)
        f.append(f"slice '{worst}' at {candidate.slices[worst]:.4f}")
    if candidate.p99_latency_ms > GATES["max_p99_latency_ms"]:
        f.append(f"p99 {candidate.p99_latency_ms}ms exceeds budget")   # the ₹22 lakh gate
    if candidate.fairness_gap > GATES["max_fairness_gap"]:
        f.append(f"fairness gap {candidate.fairness_gap:.3f}")
    return (not f), f
```

The latency gate is the one the Bengaluru team lacked. **Measure inference latency in CI**, on representative input, and treat it as a blocking criterion equal to accuracy. A model that is 4% better and 180 ms slower is usually a net loss.

Also gate on *slices*, not just aggregates. An aggregate improvement that comes with a 12-point drop on Tier-3 city applicants is not an improvement.

##### Deployment strategies

| Strategy | Traffic to new model | Detects | Risk | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Recreate** | 100% after downtime | Nothing | Very high | Low |
| **Rolling** | Gradual by pod | Crashes | Medium | Low |
| **Blue-green** | 0% → 100% instantly | Nothing pre-switch | High, but instant rollback | 2× infra |
| **Canary** | 5% → 25% → 100% | Real quality + latency issues | Low | ~1.1× |
| **Shadow** | 0% (mirrored, discarded) | Latency, errors, prediction diffs | None | 2× compute |
| **A/B** | Fixed split, statistical test | Business impact | Low | ~1.1× |

**Shadow** is the safest and most under-used. Mirror production traffic to the new model, discard its output, and compare. It validates latency, error rate and prediction distribution under *real* traffic with zero user risk. It cannot measure business impact, because nobody sees the predictions.

**Canary** routes a small real slice and watches SLOs. This is where a latency regression surfaces in minutes.

**A/B** is the only strategy that answers "does this make the business better?" — an offline NDCG gain does not guarantee a conversion gain, and sometimes contradicts it. Run A/B for at least one full weekly cycle, size the sample for your minimum detectable effect, and pre-register the primary metric so you are not fishing.

The mature sequence is all three: **shadow → canary → A/B → full rollout.**

```yaml
# Argo Rollouts: progressive canary with automated analysis
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata: {name: fraud-scorer}
spec:
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: fraud-scorer-canary
      stableService: fraud-scorer-stable
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5
        - pause: {duration: 10m}
        - analysis:
            templates: [{templateName: model-health}]
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: {duration: 30m}
        - analysis:
            templates: [{templateName: model-health}]
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: {duration: 1h}
        - setWeight: 100
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata: {name: model-health}
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      failureLimit: 2                # 2 failures -> abort and roll back
      provider:
        prometheus:
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="fraud-scorer-canary",status=~"5.."}[3m]))
            / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="fraud-scorer-canary"}[3m]))
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.01
    - name: p99-latency
      interval: 1m
      failureLimit: 2
      provider:
        prometheus:
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.99,
              sum by (le) (rate(inference_latency_bucket{service="fraud-scorer-canary"}[3m])))
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.045
    - name: score-distribution-shift
      interval: 5m
      provider:
        prometheus:
          query: |
            abs(avg(model_score{variant="canary"}) - avg(model_score{variant="stable"}))
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.02
```

That third metric — comparing the canary's mean prediction against the stable model's on concurrent traffic — is an ML-specific check with no software analogue. A model that ranks well offline but produces a wildly shifted score distribution online is signalling a feature-pipeline mismatch.

##### Continuous training

```yaml
name: continuous-training
on:
  schedule: [{cron: "0 20 * * 0"}]      # weekly, Sunday 01:30 IST
  repository_dispatch: {types: [drift-detected]}
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  train:
    runs-on: [self-hosted, gpu]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Data quality gate
        run: uv run python -m scripts.validate_snapshot --date ${{ env.SNAPSHOT }}
        # HARD STOP: never train on data that failed validation
      - name: Train candidate and retrained baseline
        run: |
          uv run python -m src.train --config conf/prod.yaml --tag candidate
          uv run python -m src.train --config conf/baseline.yaml --tag baseline
      - name: Validate gates
        run: uv run python -m scripts.validate_candidate --fail-on-regression
      - name: Register (Staging only — no auto-deploy)
        run: uv run python -m scripts.register --stage Staging
      - name: Open approval PR
        run: uv run python -m scripts.open_promotion_pr
```

Two rules make continuous training safe. **The data-quality gate blocks training**, so a broken upstream feed cannot be baked into a model. And **CT never deploys** — it registers a Staging candidate and opens a promotion request. A human approves; the CD pipeline then runs shadow and canary as usual.

##### Automated rollback

Rollback must be automatic and fast, because the whole point is that nobody is watching at 2 AM on a Sunday.

```python
ROLLBACK_TRIGGERS = {
    "error_rate":        {"threshold": 0.01,  "window_min": 3},
    "p99_latency_ms":    {"threshold": 60,    "window_min": 5},
    "score_mean_shift":  {"threshold": 0.05,  "window_min": 10},
    "null_prediction_rate": {"threshold": 0.001, "window_min": 3},
    "downstream_conversion_drop": {"threshold": -0.10, "window_min": 30},
}

def watch_and_rollback(deployment: str, model: str):
    for metric, cfg in ROLLBACK_TRIGGERS.items():
        value = query_prometheus(metric, deployment, cfg["window_min"])
        if breached(metric, value, cfg["threshold"]):
            registry.set_alias(model, "champion", registry.get_alias(model, "previous_champion"))
            k8s.rollout_undo(deployment)
            page_oncall(f"AUTO-ROLLBACK {model}: {metric}={value}")
            return True
    return False
```

Include a **business metric** (`downstream_conversion_drop`) alongside the technical ones. In the Bengaluru incident every technical metric on the model service was fine — the damage showed up in conversion, one service away. Rollback criteria that stop at the service boundary miss exactly that failure.

Rehearse rollback quarterly with a game day. Measure time-to-recovery and fix whatever makes it slow — usually model-loading time or a cache that ignores the alias change.

##### Common mistakes

- One pipeline conflating CI, CT and CD.
- No latency gate, shipping a slower model on an accuracy win.
- Gating on aggregates only, hiding a collapsed slice.
- Deploying to 100% with no canary.
- Retraining that auto-deploys.
- Training on data that failed validation.
- Comparing against a stored historical metric instead of a retrained baseline.
- Rollback that requires a human and a runbook at 2 AM.
- No business metric in the rollback criteria.
- Never testing rollback until an incident.

##### Hands-on

Build a GitHub Actions workflow with three jobs: quality (lint, types, unit tests), data contracts (schema plus a train-versus-serve feature-parity check), and smoke train on 1% of data with behavioural tests and a CML metrics comment on the PR. Then add a model-validation script with gates on aggregate metric, worst slice, latency and fairness, and prove it blocks a deliberately regressed candidate.

For the mini-project, build a full CI/CD/CT pipeline for a model service: CI as above; CT on a schedule and a drift webhook, gated on data quality, registering to Staging only; and CD running shadow deployment, then an Argo Rollouts canary with automated Prometheus analysis on error rate, latency and score-distribution shift, with automatic rollback and an on-call page. Include a quarterly rollback game-day script and record your measured time-to-recovery. Then write your comparison of canary, blue-green and shadow deployment, stating precisely what each detects, what each misses, what it costs, and when you would choose it for a model.

##### Key takeaways

- ML needs three pipelines — CI for code, CT for candidates, CD for safe deployment — and conflating them is how bad data reaches production.
- Gate on latency, worst slice and fairness, not just the aggregate metric; a 4% accuracy win at +180 ms is a loss.
- Shadow deployment validates under real traffic at zero user risk; canary catches regressions in minutes; A/B is the only test of business impact.
- Continuous training must be blocked by data-quality checks and must never auto-deploy.
- Automate rollback on technical *and* business metrics, and rehearse it before you need it.
